'''Raymond Coppinger''' (8 February 1937 – August 14, 2017) was a professor of [[cognitive science]] and biology at [[Hampshire College]]. He was an expert in dog behavior and the [[origin of the domestic dog]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Wade |first=Nicholas |date=2002-11-22 |title=From Wolf to Dog, Yes, but When? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/22/us/from-wolf-to-dog-yes-but-when.html |work=The New York Times |access-date=2020-11-13 |archive-date=2020-11-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112034718/http://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/22/us/from-wolf-to-dog-yes-but-when.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=MassLive>{{Cite web|date=2017-08-21|title=Hampshire College professor, noted dog expert, dies at 80|url=https://www.masslive.com/news/2017/08/ray_coppinger_hampshire_college.html|access-date=2020-11-18|website=masslive|language=en}}</ref>

==Education==
He majored in literature and philosophy at [[Boston University]]. He received his Ph.D. at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst|University of Massachusetts]] in biology. His thesis was on "the effect of experience and novelty on avian feeding behavior."<ref name="in-memoriam">{{Cite web|title=In Memoriam: Raymond Coppinger|url=https://www.hampshire.edu/faculty/raymond-coppinger|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201030024100/https://www.hampshire.edu/faculty/raymond-coppinger|archive-date=2020-10-30|access-date=2020-11-18|website=[[Hampshire College]]}}</ref>

==Career==
He was one of the first faculty members at Hampshire College when it was founded in 1969.<ref name="in-memoriam" />

He published more than 60&nbsp;scientific articles, and appeared in many documentaries including for the [[BBC]], the [[Canadian Broadcasting Company]], and [[PBS]].<ref name="in-memoriam" />

His wife Lorna Coppinger was a frequent collaborator on research and writing.<ref>{{cite news |last=Davis |first=Richie |date=2016-04-01 |title=What is a dog? Ray and Lorna Coppinger's new book will tell you |url=https://www.recorder.com/Life/What-is-a-dog-Ray-and-Lorna-Coppinger-s-new-book-will-tell-you-612277 |work=The Greenfield Recorder |access-date=2020-11-13 |archive-date=2016-06-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160609065228/http://www.recorder.com/Life/What-is-a-dog-Ray-and-Lorna-Coppinger-s-new-book-will-tell-you-612277 |url-status=live }}</ref> In their book "What Is a Dog?," they argue that vast majority of street dogs are not strays or lost pets, but rather well-adapted scavengers, similar to the dogs that first emerged thousands of years ago.<ref name="dogs-without-collars">{{cite news |last=Gorman |first=James |date=2016-04-18 |title=The World is Full of Dogs Without Collars |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/19/science/the-world-is-full-of-dogswithout-collars.html |work=The New York Times |access-date=2020-11-13 |archive-date=2020-11-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111101815/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/19/science/the-world-is-full-of-dogswithout-collars.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Livestock Dog Project===
The Coppingers compiled data for ten years from over 1,400 [[Livestock guardian dog|Livestock Guardian Dogs]] (LGDs) to research their use on American ranches to combat coyotes. Their work is still the single largest, long term study of LGDs.{{cn|date=February 2026}} He and his wife helped develop and popularize the [[Anatolian Shepherd]] breed in the United States.<ref name="dogs-without-collars" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-08-24|title=Editorial: The impact of Hampshire College's alums and faculty|url=https://www.gazettenet.com/Editorial-Celebrating-Hampshire-College-alum-Paul-Bockelman-s-community-leadership-mourning-founding-faculty-member-Raymond-Coppinger-s-death-12023944|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170826102413/http://www.gazettenet.com/Editorial-Celebrating-Hampshire-College-alum-Paul-Bockelman-s-community-leadership-mourning-founding-faculty-member-Raymond-Coppinger-s-death-12023944|archive-date=2017-08-26|access-date=2020-11-18|website=Daily Hampshire Gazette}}</ref>

===Foxes===
His research on foxes has challenged views about [[domestication syndrome]] with [[fox]]es, suggesting that the traits associated with the syndrome occurred in the fox population prior to their domestication.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gorman|first=James|date=2019-12-03|title=Why Are These Foxes Tame? Maybe They Weren't So Wild to Begin With|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/03/science/foxes-tame-belyaev.html|access-date=2020-11-18|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2020-11-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111215758/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/03/science/foxes-tame-belyaev.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=MacLean|first=Colin|title=A discovery at a small P.E.I. museum is challenging decades-old scientific research about domesticated foxes|url=http://www.saltwire.com/news/canada/how-a-sleepy-summerside-museum-sparked-an-international-argument-about-domesticated-foxes-405489/|access-date=2020-11-18|website=www.saltwire.com|language=en|archive-date=2020-11-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201118202503/https://www.saltwire.com/news/canada/how-a-sleepy-summerside-museum-sparked-an-international-argument-about-domesticated-foxes-405489/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Death==
Coppinger died at the age of 80, from cancer. He is survived by his wife, Lorna.<ref name=MassLive/>
